newsitem.title: USA: Black farmers ask fair deal in U.S. loan programs.
newsitem.headline: Black farmers ask fair deal in U.S. loan programs.

text.p: Fifty black farmers rallied in front of the White House Thursday, calling on President Clinton to assure fair treatment for them in agricultural lending programs.
They contended black farmers endure discrimination in Agriculture Department lending programs and that racism was the basis for loan rejections and foreclosures.
"We want to talk to Bill Clinton today," said John Boyd, president of the National Black Farmers Association. "We can't wait. We're tired of putting things off."
James Myart, lawyer for the NBFA, said James Gilliland, the Agriculture Department's top lawyer, should be replaced. "We want a civil rights lawyer as general counsel."

The group was scheduled to meet Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman Thursday to discuss their complaints. Before the meeting, Glickman announced the formation of a civil rights action team to report by mid-February on "ways to solve existing problems."
"Today...civil rights compliance has shifted into overdrive," Glickman said in a statement. "I am devoted to solving this department's civil rights problems -- both inside and outside."
Glickman personally told the department's top executives to make civil rights compliance their top priority.

Earlier in the week, Glickman directed the department's inspector general to investigate complaints of discrimination in farm loans. He also ordered the creation of "outreach" offices for agencies dealing with farmers.
There are about 19,000 black-run farms in the United States among nearly two million farms. The number of black farms has declined far more rapidly than the overall U.S. figure in recent years.
A 1990 U.S. House report described black farming as nearing extinction. Blacks tend to own smaller farms, a sector that faces great financial stress.
